extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing objective (secondary) evidence of nonobviousness and related issues (unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need, copying, operability, enablement) during patent examination and prosecution. Covers how to weigh, compare, and require evidence and declarations/affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected properties significance relative to expected properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the unexpected properties of a claimed invention are not shown to have a significance equal to or greater than the expected properties, the evidence of unexpected properties may not be sufficient to rebut the evidence of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claimed unexpected advantages (e.g., lower peak discharge current, higher luminous efficiency) are less significant than expected improvements (e.g., higher memory margin, lower operating voltage), they may fail to rebut a prima facie obviousness case (In re Nolan; In re Eli Lilly). Examiner should compare the relative significance of expected vs. unexpected properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness of a claimed invention, just as unexpected results are evidence of unobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a beneficial result would have been expected based on prior art teachings, that result supports obviousness (In re Gershon; Ex parte Blanc). Examples include expected decreases in enamel solubility or expected antioxidant effectiveness taught by references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support; the showing must be reviewed to see if the results occur over the entire claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If tests demonstrate unexpected results only at limited points that do not cover the full claimed range (e.g., claims spanning 60°C+ but tests only at 110°C and 130°C may be insufficient if claimed range includes lower temperatures), the evidence may fail (In re Clemens; In re Peterson; In re Grasselli). Examiner should assess whether data spans the claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness of a genus can be supported by species data when trend allows extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The nonobviousness of a broader claimed range may be supported by evidence based on unexpected results of a species or narrower range if one of ordinary skill would be able to determine a trend allowing reasonable extension of the probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited exemplification can support a genus if data show a trend that reasonably predicts similar results across the genus (In re Kollman). Conversely, isolated or unrepresentative species data that do not permit reasonable extrapolation are insufficient (In re Lindner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating criticality of a claimed range requires sufficient tests inside and outside the range
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish unexpected results over a claimed range, applicants should compare a sufficient number of tests both inside and outside the claimed range to show the criticality of the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative testing must be adequate to show a claimed range is critical (In re Hill). Examiners look for tests that demonstrate sharp changes or critical boundaries across claimed values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration must compare claimed subject matter with closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons should determine number and importance of claim limitations in common with references (In re Burckel; In re Merchant). Deviations from reference disclosures should be explained (In re Finley) or noted and evaluated (In re Armstrong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant may compare claimed invention with prior art closer than that applied by the examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may compare the claimed invention with prior art that is more closely related to the invention than the prior art relied upon by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence comparing to closer references can rebut a rejection based on less-relevant prior art (In re Holladay; Ex parte Humber). Applicants should present comparisons to the most relevant art available.

rubrics_metrics.name: When two equally close prior art references exist, single-reference testing may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing unexpected results over one of two equally close prior art references will not rebut prima facie obviousness unless the teachings of the prior art references are sufficiently similar that testing one would provide equivalent information about the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant does not have to test every compound taught by each reference, but when testing fewer than all cited compounds, tests must be sufficient to permit conclusions about relative effectiveness across the closest prior art (In re Johnson; quoting In re Payne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison limited to prior art that actually exists
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention may be compared with the closest subject matter that exists in the prior art; applicant is not required to compare with subject matter that does not exist in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is improper to require comparison with hypothetical or constructed combinations of references that would amount to comparing the invention with an invention that does not exist in the prior art (In re Geiger; In re Chapman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider advantages not disclosed in the specification as part of the totality of the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded; the totality of the record (including prosecution evidence) should be considered in determining obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages demonstrated during prosecution (even if not disclosed in the spec) should be evaluated when they rebut obviousness (In re Chu). The specification need not disclose proportions or values for applicants to present evidence of criticality (In re Saunders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations/affidavits required; publications do not substitute for sworn testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason for requiring evidence in declaration or affidavit form is to obtain assurances statements are correct; permitting a publication to substitute for expert testimony would circumvent statutory guarantees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications may be probative evidence but do not replace properly executed affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 (Ex parte Gray). Examiners should require sworn statements where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus required between claimed invention and evidence of commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of proof of establishing a nexus between the claimed invention and the evidence of commercial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO relies on applicants to provide hard evidence of commercial success and nexus because the examiner lacks means to gather such evidence (In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen). Nexus denotes a factually and legally sufficient connection (Demaco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success abroad is relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success abroad, as well as in the United States, is relevant in resolving the issue of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign sales and market acceptance may be considered (Lindemann Maschinenfabrik GMBH v. American Hoist & Derrick Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness including commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of commercial success for a narrower product (e.g., 'cups') does not support broad claims (e.g., 'containers') (In re Tiffin). Commercial success must be due to claimed features, not unclaimed aspects (Joy Technologies v. Manbeck). Declarations that a sold product is 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' are insufficient without showing the sold product corresponds to the claimed invention (Ex parte Standish).

rubrics_metrics.name: When commercial product is not coextensive with claimed invention, show legally sufficient relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: If a commercially successful product or process is not coextensive with the claimed invention, applicant must show a legally sufficient relationship between the claimed feature and the commercial product or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial success at typical points within claimed ranges can be persuasive if affidavits indicate operation throughout the range approximates that point (In re Hollingsworth; Demaco). Applicant must tie the commercial success to the claimed feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must be derived from the claimed invention (not advertising or extraneous factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success alleged must be directly derived from the invention claimed, and not the result of heavy promotion, advertising, purchaser ties, or other business events extraneous to the merits of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions that increased sales are due to the invention require evidentiary support; inventor opinions are insufficient (In re Mageli; In re Huang). Licensing or advertising may inflate apparent success for reasons unrelated to unobviousness (Pentec; EWP Corp. v. Reliance). Examiners must scrutinize causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must flow from functions/advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success must not be attributable to modifications made by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a commercially successful embodiment's success arises from unclaimed modifications or third-party improvements, the evidence is less probative (In re Vamco Machine & Tool, Inc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: In design cases, nexus between commercial success and design is especially difficult
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a nexus between commercial success and the claimed design is especially difficult; evidence must clearly attribute success to the design rather than brand recognition, improved performance, or other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patents require clear attribution of sales/market acceptance to the design itself (Litton Systems v. Whirlpool). Examiners should require tight causal linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales figures must be adequately defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross sales figures do not alone show commercial success absent evidence as to market share, time period of sales, or normal expected sales in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide market share, relevant time period, and baseline expectations to make sales figures probative (Cable Electric Products v. Genmark; Ex parte Standish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need and failure of others: need must be recognized, persistent, and unsolved
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must satisfy a long-felt need which was recognized, persistent, and not solved by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must show the problem was recognized in the art and that others attempted but failed to solve it; if the problem was first recognized by the applicant or already solved by others, long-felt need is weak (In re Gershon; Orthopedic Equipment Co. v. All Orthopedic Appliances; Newell v. Kenney).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need measured from date problem identified and efforts made to solve it
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-felt need is analyzed as of the date the problem is identified and articulated, and there is evidence of efforts to solve it, not as of the date of the most pertinent prior art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate long-felt need using the timeline when the problem and solution efforts became known (Texas Instruments v. ITC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider other factors that may explain failure of others to solve need
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure of others to solve a need may be due to lack of interest or lack of appreciation of potential/marketability rather than lack of technical know-how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess alternative explanations for apparent failure to solve (Scully Signal Co.; Environmental Designs v. Union Oil). Licensing by arm's-length parties may add weight to affidavits (In re Tiffin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of experts before invention is strong evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of disbelief by experts, expressed before inventors proved them wrong, constitute strong evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior expert incredulity and years of research supporting the invention can rebut prima facie obviousness (Environmental Designs v. Union Oil; In re Dow Chemical Co.; Burlington Industries v. Quigg). Examiners should consider contemporaneous expert skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying may support nonobviousness but requires more than mere copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that competitors copied the invention can support nonobviousness, but more than the mere fact of copying is necessary; copying may be due to non-technical factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying is persuasive when an alleged infringer tried for a substantial time to design its own solution and failed, then copied (Dow Chem. Co. v. American Cyanamid). Copying that is not identical or where the other party did not expend effort is less persuasive (Pentec; Vandenberg; Panduit). Examiners should evaluate the effort and context of copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should not opine on operability of a patent; affidavits attacking operability must rebut presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent is presumed valid, including a presumption of operability; affidavits or declarations attacking operability of a patent cited as reference must rebut the presumption of operability by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere showing that one can operate within a disclosure without obtaining the alleged product does not overcome the presumption (In re Weber). Failures of uninterested experimenters carry less weight. Assertions of inoperability limited to features not relied upon do not negate other operative features of the reference (In re Sasse; In re Shepherd; In re Michalek; In re Reid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and operability guidance: when to require and how to evaluate evidence under 35 U.S.C. 101
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when it is proper to require evidence of utility or operativeness and how to evaluate submitted evidence to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2107.02 and § 2107-§2107.03 for procedures and precedent for utility/operability determinations. Examiners may require evidence and evaluate it under established standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure/enablement: burden on applicant after prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the examiner has established a prima facie case of lack of enablement, the burden falls on the applicant to present persuasive arguments, supported by suitable proofs where necessary, that one skilled in the art could make and use the invention from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence supplementing a deficient specification must establish that missing information would have been known to those of ordinary skill (In re Brandstadter; In re Howarth). Affidavits explaining how to construct elements not described are generally not sufficient (In re Buchner; In re Smyth). Affidavits purporting merely to interpret a disclosure are usually not considered, though opinion testimony explaining factual bases may be helpful on a case-by-case basis (In re Oppenauer; Glaser v. Strickland).
